ch2_p9_cascade_sim_solo.text: Welcome to the Ingestion Quality Cost Cascade Workbench. Adjust monthly ingestion volume, per-stage defect rates, and leakage fractions to evaluate the financial return on investment of upstream pre-ingestion assertion gates.

ch2_p9_cascade_sim_duo.text: Try sliding the ingestion volume up to ten million records and adjusting leakage to thirty percent. Look at how downstream failure costs skyrocket compared to the cheap upstream assertion gate!

ch2_p9_chk1_solo.text: Active Checkpoint 1: The 1-10-100 Cost Cascade Arithmetic. Calculate the net monthly financial savings of enforcing upstream pre-ingestion validation over allowing twenty percent defect leakage into production billing.

ch2_p9_chk1_duo.text: Checkpoint 1! Twenty-five thousand corrupt records. Warehouse remediation costs ten thousand dollars, and billing outage repair costs twenty-five thousand. What is the net monthly saving?

ch2_p9_chk1_feedback_correct.text: Spot on! Option B is correct. Without upstream validation, cleaning eighty percent in the warehouse costs ten thousand dollars, and repairing twenty percent in billing costs twenty-five thousand, totaling thirty-five thousand. Upstream validation costs only twelve hundred and fifty dollars, securing thirty-three thousand seven hundred and fifty dollars in net monthly savings, or four hundred and five thousand dollars annually. That is a 28x return on investment.

ch2_p9_chk1_feedback_incorrect.text: Incorrect. Review the 1-10-100 cascade arithmetic: twenty-five thousand corrupt records times five cents is twelve hundred and fifty dollars for upstream validation. But letting twenty percent leak into billing costs twenty-five thousand dollars plus ten thousand in warehouse cleaning, totaling thirty-five thousand. Subtracting twelve hundred and fifty yields thirty-three thousand seven hundred and fifty dollars in net monthly savings. The correct answer is Option B.

ch2_p9_heckman_sim_solo.text: Welcome to the Heckman Selection Bias and Inverse Mills Ratio Workbench. Vary the latent error correlation rho and selection threshold gamma to observe how Heckman's two-step estimator eliminates endogenous sample selection bias.

ch2_p9_heckman_sim_duo.text: Look at the naive slope when rho is positive zero point seven! It jumps up to 3.22, almost thirty percent higher than ground truth. But Heckman's correction brings it right back to 2.50!

ch2_p9_chk2_solo.text: Active Checkpoint 2: Heckman Selection and the Truncation Hazard Invariant. In observational telemetry, under what condition does the Inverse Mills Ratio lambda approach zero, eliminating selection bias without econometric adjustment?

ch2_p9_chk2_duo.text: Active Checkpoint 2! When does the hazard rate lambda of alpha approach zero? Think about what happens when almost the entire population participates in the dataset.

ch2_p9_chk2_feedback_correct.text: Masterful derivation! Option B is correct. The Inverse Mills Ratio lambda equals phi of alpha divided by Phi of alpha, representing the conditional expectation of the unobserved shock given selection. As sampling inclusion approaches certainty, Phi approaches one, and the density phi in the tail approaches zero, causing lambda to vanish. In fully saturated samples, selection bias disappears.

ch2_p9_chk2_feedback_incorrect.text: Incorrect. Remember the definition of the Inverse Mills Ratio: lambda equals phi of alpha divided by Phi of alpha. As inclusion probability Phi approaches one, the selection threshold moves far into the tail, causing density phi to approach zero. Thus lambda approaches zero and selection bias vanishes in saturated cohorts. The correct answer is Option B.
